title: KANO: Kolmogorov-Arnold Neural Operator
claim: The standard spectral-only operator layer is replaced by a dual-domain learnable-basis architecture that handles position-dependent dynamics.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, parallel skip branches with math labels on arrows
description: Two side-by-side block diagrams, labeled (a) and (b). Panel (a) shows the FNO layer. Input 'a' in a circle splits into two branches. The top branch goes through an orange box R_θ(ξ), annotated with the Fourier-domain formula F^{-1}[R_θ(ξ)·F_m]a(x). The bottom branch goes through an orange box W, labeled W·a(x). Both feed an orange tall '+' box, then an orange σ circle, then a white circle holding L_FNO(a). Panel (b) shows the KANO layer. Input 'a' splits in two. The top branch goes through a small KAN-style network drawing that outputs p_θ(x, ξ), then through a second network drawing labeled Op_m(p)a(x). The bottom branch passes a(x) straight through. Both branches meet at the second network, which feeds a white circle holding L_KANO(a). Panel (a) is filled with orange; panel (b) uses black-and-white network sketches. The eye goes first to the orange blocks on the left.
caption: (a) $\ten{L}_{\tiny{FNO}}$ architecture. (b) $\ten{L}_{\tiny{KANO}}$ architecture.
abstract: We introduce Kolmogorov--Arnold Neural Operator (KANO), a dual-domain neural operator jointly parameterized by both spectral and spatial bases with intrinsic symbolic interpretability. We theoretically demonstrate that KANO overcomes the pure-spectral bottleneck of Fourier Neural Operator (FNO): KANO remains expressive over generic position-dependent dynamics (variable coefficient PDEs) for any physical input, whereas FNO stays practical only for spectrally sparse operators and strictly imposes a fast-decaying input Fourier tail. We verify our claims empirically on position-dependent differential operators, for which KANO robustly generalizes but FNO fails to. In the quantum Hamiltonian learning benchmark, KANO reconstructs ground-truth Hamiltonians in closed-form symbolic representations accurate to the fourth decimal place in coefficients and attains $\approx 6\times10^{-6}$ state infidelity from projective measurement data, substantially outperforming that of the FNO trained with ideal full wave function data, $\approx 1.5\times10^{-2}$, by orders of magnitude.
